text:
The Case for the Joined Hand

Every few years someone proposes that primary schools stop teaching joined-up handwriting. The argument is easy to make. Adults type almost everything, children will type even more, and the hours spent coaxing seven-year-olds to loop an f could go to coding, or reading, or simply more maths. Finland dropped its cursive requirement in 2016. The American Common Core standards of 2010 left it out altogether. On the face of it, joined handwriting looks like the fountain pen or the slide rule: a skill kept alive by nostalgia.

I think that view is wrong, and that primary schools should keep teaching children to join their letters. The reason is not tradition, and it is not that cursive has special powers. The reason is that fluent handwriting still does real work in a child's education, and joining is how handwriting becomes fluent.

Start with what handwriting is for at primary age. It is not mainly a way of producing documents. It is part of how children learn to read and spell. When a child forms a letter by hand, they must recall its shape, plan a sequence of strokes and execute it, and that effort seems to fix the letter in memory in a way that pressing a key does not. Brain-imaging studies by Karin James and colleagues found that pre-literate children who had practised writing letters by hand showed activity in reading-related brain regions when they later looked at those letters, while children who had typed or traced them did not. EEG work by Audrey van der Meer's group in Norway has found more widespread patterns of brain connectivity during handwriting than during typing. These studies are small, and they should not be oversold, but they point the same way as decades of classroom experience: children who write letters learn letters.

That is an argument for handwriting, not specifically for joining it. So here is the second step. Handwriting only helps a child if it becomes automatic. A pupil who has to think about how to form each letter has little attention left for what they want to say. Working memory is limited, and in a young writer it is being asked to hold a sentence, spell its words, remember the punctuation and move the pencil all at once. Research on children's composition, notably by Virginia Berninger and Steve Graham, has repeatedly found that handwriting fluency predicts the length and quality of what children write, and that teaching handwriting explicitly improves their writing, not just its appearance. The pencil is a bottleneck. Widen it and the ideas get through.

Joining is the standard way of widening it. Printing separate letters means lifting the pen dozens of times a line, and each lift is a small stop and restart. A joined hand keeps the pen moving, lets the writer treat common letter strings as single gestures, and builds a rhythm that carries the word along. It also helps with a problem any primary teacher will recognise: children who print often space their letters so evenly that words run together, whereas a joined word is visibly a unit. Spelling benefits for the same reason. A child who writes "ight" as one movement a few hundred times has a motor memory of the pattern to go with the visual one.

Here I should concede what the evidence does not show. Studies comparing the speed of pure cursive with pure print are mixed, and some find that the fastest writers use a hybrid, joining some letters and not others. Nobody has demonstrated that a fully looped copperplate makes children cleverer. But this concession helps the case more than it hurts it. The hybrid hand that fast adult writers settle into is something they arrive at after being taught to join; they keep the joins that are efficient and drop the ones that are not. A child never taught to join does not get that choice. The sensible aim, and the one England's national curriculum actually sets, is not ornamental script. It is a legible, fluent, comfortable hand, in which pupils learn the joins and also learn which letters are best left unjoined. That is a modest, practical goal, and it is the one worth defending.

The strongest objection is that all of this is solving a problem typing has already solved. If automaticity is the point, why not make children automatic at the keyboard instead? The answer is partly developmental and partly practical. Touch-typing requires coordinating ten fingers across a layout with no relation to letter shapes, and most children are not ready to learn it properly until seven or eight at the earliest; before that they hunt and peck, which is slower than handwriting and teaches them nothing about letter formation. Reading instruction cannot wait that long. In the years when children are learning what letters are, the pencil is the right tool.

Later on, the picture is closer, but handwriting keeps advantages. The well-known 2014 study by Mueller and Oppenheimer, which found that students taking notes by hand understood lectures better than those typing, has had a rocky replication record, and I would not rest the case on it. A plainer point survives. Writing by hand is slower than typing, which forces the note-taker to select and compress, and a page of handwritten notes allows arrows, diagrams, marginal additions and equations with no friction at all. A great deal of school work, especially in mathematics and science, is not linear text and is awkward on a keyboard. And a device that can take notes can also do everything else a device does. Paper offers no notifications.

Then there is the blunt fact of examinations. In Britain and in many other countries, pupils still sit most of their public exams with a pen, writing for two or three hours at a stretch. That may change, but it has been about to change for twenty years. As long as it holds, a child with a slow, effortful hand is at a real disadvantage: they write less, tire sooner, and spend attention on the pen that their competitors spend on the question. Moving exams on screen would not remove the difficulty, either. It would shift the advantage toward children with good keyboards and long practice at home.

That leads to equity, which is usually claimed by the other side. The argument runs that handwriting drills penalise children with poor motor control and that technology levels the field. For children with dyspraxia or specific difficulties, a keyboard is indeed the right accommodation, and schools should offer it readily. But for the majority the equity argument cuts the opposite way. A pencil and paper cost almost nothing, need no charging, and are the same in every home. Handwriting taught well at school is a skill a child owns regardless of what their family can buy. If schools stop teaching it, the children of parents who care about it will still learn, at the kitchen table or from a tutor, and the others will not. Abandoning a cheap universal skill rarely helps the poor.

There is also the question of what is being given up to make room. The time involved is small. Good practice is something like ten or fifteen minutes a day in the early years, tapering off once the hand is secure, and much of it doubles as spelling practice. The countries and states that dropped cursive did not obviously gain anything from the saved minutes, and several have reversed course. More than twenty American states have brought cursive requirements back, California among them in 2024. Some of the reasoning behind those laws is sentimental, the worry that children will be unable to read the Declaration of Independence or their grandmother's letters. That is a minor argument, but not an empty one. A person who cannot read joined writing is cut off from most handwritten documents before the late twentieth century, and from a good many of the notes that older relatives, doctors and colleagues still produce.

The last point is harder to measure, and I offer it without statistics. Learning to write a joined hand is one of the first things a child does that takes sustained practice over years and yields a visible, personal result. No two hands come out the same. Children are proud of the pen licence, the first neat page, the signature they invent. Education has room for a few skills whose value lies partly in the discipline of acquiring them, and this one is cheap, quiet and useful as well.

None of this is an argument against teaching typing. Children need both, and schools should teach touch-typing properly from the middle of primary school instead of assuming children pick it up. The choice between pen and keyboard is a false one. The real question is whether, in the years when children are learning to read, spell and put sentences together, we should still teach them a fast and fluent hand. The evidence that handwriting supports literacy is good, the evidence that fluency supports composition is better, and joining is the ordinary route to fluency. The cost is a few minutes a day. Schools should keep paying it.
